desc: NASA was created by the National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 as an explicitly civilian agency, and for six decades its institutional answer on UFOs was that the subject belonged to the Air Force. That changed on 9 June 2022, when NASA announced an independent study of unidentified anomalous phenomena, and on 14 September 2023, when it published the 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Independent Study Team Report'. The 16-member panel was chaired by Dr David Spergel of the Simons Foundation and included Dr Anamaria Berea, Dr Federica Bianco, Dr David Grinspoon and the retired NASA astronaut Captain Scott Kelly. The report's findings are notable less for what they concluded about UAP than for what they conceded about the data problem: that 'much of the data collected by military sensors or intelligence satellites are classified', that structured data curation 'plays a pivotal role' and is largely absent, and that NASA's Earth-observing fleet and the U.S. commercial remote-sensing industry have 'the collective potential to directly resolve UAP events'. In the foreword, Associate Administrator for the Science Mission Directorate Dr Nicola Fox announced that 'NASA is appointing a Director of UAP Research to centralize communications'. NASA's leverage on this board is that it is the one agency with world-class sensing capability, a statutory public mission and no SAP equity in the alleged recovery enterprise - which makes it the most plausible venue for an unclassified evidentiary standard, and the agency most conspicuously kept at arm's length from the classified holdings.

claims.text: On 14 September 2023, under release 23-106, NASA published the UAP Independent Study Team final report and announced the appointment of Mark McInerney as director of UAP research.

The independent study team was chaired by David Spergel, president of the Simons Foundation, and comprised sixteen experts; it was set up outside NASA and used unclassified data from civilian government entities, commercial data and other sources.
Spergel stated: 'Using unclassified data was essential for our team's fact-finding, open-communication collaboration, and for upholding scientific rigor to produce this report for NASA.'
NASA states in the same release that 'The report is not a review or assessment of previous UAP incidents' — the study's charter excluded the historical record.

Mark McInerney 'previously served as NASA's liaison to the Department of Defense covering limited UAP activities for the agency,' and has held positions at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, NOAA and the National Hurricane Center since 1996. Administrator Bill Nelson said the new director would apply 'artificial intelligence and machine learning to search the skies for anomalies' and that 'NASA will do this work transparently for the benefit of humanity.'

claims.text: NASA's Office of Communications stated in 2025: 'Per the requirements in Section 1841-1842 of the Fiscal Year 2024 National Defense Authorization Act for handling records related to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), NASA does not have any records that meet the requirements to submit records to the National Archives. Any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense.'

The only agencies that added UAP records to the National Archives online catalog (Record Group 615) during 2025 were the FAA, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the NSA, ODNI and the Office of the Secretary of Defense; NASA was not among them, despite a statutory transfer deadline of 30 September 2025.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman stated on 27 May 2026: 'What's being surfaced isn't crashed ships or alien bodies, but real unexplained phenomena.'
Isaacman stated: 'There's nothing I'm aware of in terms of alien bodies or spaceships.' — a personal-knowledge formulation rather than an institutional denial.

Isaacman stated that federal agencies did not conduct UAP records searches until compelled: 'Government agencies really didn't take this quite as seriously in the past until President Trump put out the tweet, basically giving an order to government agencies and going out and saying, look, this time you better go through the files, you better start searching your databases and bring things up.'

Isaacman identified NASA's own most significant contribution to the disclosure: 'I would say that some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure was taken on the surface of the moon from Apollo 12 and 17. You can't be a moon landing denier and also believe that those photos captured unexplained phenomenon.'

The PURSUE releases include astronaut and NASA-related accounts from the Apollo and Gemini eras describing strange lights and unidentified objects observed in space, alongside infrared footage from 2023 of an F-16 engaging a diamond-shaped object over Lake Huron and reports of unexplained objects near military operations in Iran, Syria, Iraq and Greece.

The Department of War's PURSUE Release 05 slideshow (7 August 2026) carries an image captioned as 'A photograph of an unidentified object in low-Earth orbit, taken from Space Shuttle Columbia in 1996' while the underlying file is named DOW-UAP-D098_Film-Analysis-of-Unidentified-Objects_1953.jpg — a 43-year date discrepancy inside the government's own release metadata.

Marc Millis, a former NASA propulsion engineer and founder of the Tau Zero Foundation, was among the authors of the 38 Defense Intelligence Reference Documents produced under the DIA's AAWSAP/AATIP contract to Bigelow Aerospace.

dossier.denialPosture: NASA's denial operates in three layers, each with an escape hatch. The 2023 Independent Study Team found no evidence of extraterrestrial origin while working exclusively from unclassified data and explicitly excluding past incidents from its charter. The 2025 Office of Communications statement denies possession of transferable records by asserting DoD ownership rather than absence — a custody argument, not a factual one. And Administrator Isaacman's 2026 formulation, 'There's nothing I'm aware of in terms of alien bodies or spaceships,' limits the denial to the personal knowledge of an appointee with no read-in to the compartments in question. Each is technically defensible and none touches the underlying question.
dossier.narrative:
NASA entered the modern UAP file formally in 2022, when it commissioned an outside Independent Study Team to advise on how the agency might contribute. The team's final report was published on 14 September 2023 under NASA release 23-106, chaired by David Spergel, president of the Simons Foundation, with sixteen members. Its overall recommendation was that NASA play a prominent role in the whole-of-government effort by using its open-source resources, technological expertise, data analysis techniques, federal and commercial partnerships, and Earth-observing assets to curate a better dataset for understanding future UAP. The report explicitly is not a review or assessment of previous UAP incidents. That boundary is the point: NASA's charter for the study excluded the historical record, which is where the legacy program question lives.

Spergel described the methodological constraint as a virtue: "Using unclassified data was essential for our team's fact-finding, open-communication collaboration, and for upholding scientific rigor to produce this report for NASA." The team reported that there are currently a limited number of high-quality observations of UAP, which make it impossible to draw firm scientific conclusions about their nature. The same architecture reappears three years later in the UAP Science Advisory Council chaired by Avi Loeb — unclassified data only, chartered to recommend how to get better data, structurally incapable of reaching a custody finding. NASA built the template.

With the report NASA named Mark McInerney its Director of UAP Research. McInerney had previously served as NASA's liaison to the Department of Defense "covering limited UAP activities for the agency" — meaning the agency's UAP function had already existed as a DoD liaison billet before it was given a public title. Administrator Bill Nelson framed the role in terms of instrumentation and analytics: the director would apply "artificial intelligence and machine learning to search the skies for anomalies," and "NASA will do this work transparently for the benefit of humanity." McInerney's career runs through NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, NOAA and the National Hurricane Center since 1996 — a NOAA lineage he shares with Tim Gallaudet, the retired admiral now on the 2026 UAP Science Advisory Council.

Then came the records question, and with it the most consequential NASA statement in the public record. The FY2024 NDAA, sections 1841-1842, required federal agencies to identify and transfer UAP records to a new collection at the National Archives, with digital transfers due by 30 September 2025. Record Group 615 was created to hold them. Over the course of 2025 the FAA, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the National Security Agency, ODNI and the Office of the Secretary of Defense transferred records into the online catalog. NASA did not. Asked why, NASA's Office of Communications replied: "Per the requirements in Section 1841-1842 of the Fiscal Year 2024 National Defense Authorization Act for handling records related to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), NASA does not have any records that meet the requirements to submit records to the National Archives. Any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense." That is not a denial of possession. It is an assertion of foreign ownership over material NASA holds — a jurisdictional argument that keeps agency UAP records outside a statutory public-release regime by routing their custody back into the Department of War.

The 2026 disclosure wave then produced the contradiction. On 27 May 2026, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Fox News Digital that the newly declassified files show "real unexplained phenomena" but no recovered craft: "What's being surfaced isn't crashed ships or alien bodies, but real unexplained phenomena," and "There's nothing I'm aware of in terms of alien bodies or spaceships." Note the construction — personal awareness, from a political appointee without read-in to the compartments where such material would be held. In the same interview Isaacman said agencies "really didn't take this quite as seriously in the past until President Trump put out the tweet, basically giving an order to government agencies and going out and saying, look, this time you better go through the files, you better start searching your databases and bring things up" — a sitting NASA Administrator stating that federal agencies did not conduct records searches for UAP material until a presidential post compelled them.

And on NASA's own contribution: "I would say that some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure was taken on the surface of the moon from Apollo 12 and 17. You can't be a moon landing denier and also believe that those photos captured unexplained phenomenon." Fox News reported that the PURSUE material includes astronaut and NASA-related accounts from the Apollo and Gemini eras describing strange lights and unidentified objects observed in space, alongside 2023 infrared footage of an F-16 engaging a diamond-shaped object over Lake Huron and reports from military operations in Iran, Syria, Iraq and Greece. Set against the 2025 Office of Communications statement — NASA has no qualifying records because DoD owns them — the position is that NASA's most interesting UAP data was released through the Department of War's website rather than deposited in the National Archives collection Congress created for exactly that purpose. One route is statutory, permanent and indexed; the other is a rolling, discretionary web publication controlled by the Secretary of War. NASA's material went down the second.

A loose thread worth pulling: on the war.gov PURSUE page, the Release 05 slideshow of 7 August 2026 carries an image described as "A photograph of an unidentified object in low-Earth orbit, taken from Space Shuttle Columbia in 1996," while the underlying file is named DOW-UAP-D098_Film-Analysis-of-Unidentified-Objects_1953.jpg. A 1996 Columbia photograph filed under a 1953 film analysis is either a metadata error or an indexing artifact, and either way it is a checkable discrepancy in the government's own release. The Columbia 1996 imagery in question is almost certainly from STS-75, the tethered satellite mission whose downlink footage has been argued over for thirty years — meaning the 2026 disclosure has quietly placed a long-contested NASA video into an official unresolved-case release.
openQuestions: What UAP-related records does NASA physically hold that it characterises as DoD-owned, and who at NASA made that ownership determination?
Was NASA's ownership position coordinated with the Department of Defense or the National Archives, and is there written correspondence recording it?
Is Mark McInerney still serving as Director of UAP Research under Administrator Isaacman, and has the role been budgeted or staffed?
Why does PURSUE Release 05 file DOW-UAP-D098 carry a 1953 film-analysis filename while being described as a 1996 Space Shuttle Columbia photograph, and is the underlying imagery from STS-75?
Where are the original Apollo 12 and Apollo 17 lunar-surface negatives and the associated frame indices, and were any frames withheld from the PURSUE release?
Did the NASA Independent Study Team request classified access and, if so, who denied it?
Which NASA Gemini- and Apollo-era astronaut accounts entered PURSUE, through what channel, and were the astronauts or their estates consulted?
dossier.whatItIs: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the U.S. civil space agency. Since 2022 it has been a formal participant in the government's UAP effort through a commissioned Independent Study Team, whose final report it published on 14 September 2023 alongside the appointment of a Director of UAP Research. Since 2026 it has been a contributing agency to the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters, supplying Apollo- and Gemini-era imagery and astronaut accounts.
dossier.whyImplicated: NASA's role in the concealment architecture is not custody; it is certification. It is the civilian, scientifically credentialed institution that repeatedly states there is no evidence of extraterrestrial origin while holding, by its own design choices, no access to the compartmented material where the question would actually be settled — its Independent Study Team used unclassified data only, and its charter expressly excluded review of past incidents. The sharper fact is a custody claim. In 2025 NASA's Office of Communications told a records researcher that it has no UAP records qualifying for transfer to the National Archives under the FY2024 NDAA because "any agency-related records associated with UAP, came from, and are owned by, the U.S. Department of Defense." That single sentence removes NASA's UAP holdings from the statutory records regime by attributing ownership to the department least likely to release them. Ten months later NASA's own Administrator publicly identified NASA-provided Apollo 12 and Apollo 17 lunar-surface imagery as "some of the most interesting data that NASA has provided as part of the UAP disclosure." Both statements cannot sit comfortably together: an agency with nothing to transfer, holding the most interesting data.
